subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: Karthik, you slammed that door so hard the calendar fell. Let your Farida Nani tell you something. When I was ten, my brother Yunus and I fought over whose turn it was with the radio. He won, because he was older and louder. I stamped across the courtyard so hard my anklets rang, and I slammed the kitchen door. My Abba didn't shout. That evening he said, “Next time, stamp all the way to the mango tree. Touch it. Walk back slowly. Then talk.” At the next fight, I did it. By the time I came back, the fire in my chest had gone down, and I could say, “It's not fair, you always choose.” Yunus actually listened.

qa.q: What did Farida and Yunus fight over?
qa.a: They fought over whose turn it was with the radio.

qa.q: What was young Farida feeling when she stamped across the courtyard?
qa.a: She felt angry and powerless after losing to her older, louder brother, and needed to get away.

qa.q: What choice did Farida make in the next fight, and why did it help?
qa.a: She walked to the mango tree and back before talking, which let her anger cool so she could say calmly what felt unfair.

qa.q: How might Yunus have experienced the calmer Farida?
qa.a: Yunus probably found it easier to listen to a calm complaint than to a slammed door.

grounding: Shows a child stamping and slamming out after losing an argument, and a walk-then-talk routine turning the impulse into a safe boundary.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: The rain had kept everyone inside the one-room flat for three days. When Gautam won the argument over the TV remote again, Ganga jumped up, stamped her foot so hard the steel glasses rattled, and headed for the door. Then she stopped. Outside was a wall of rain. There was nowhere to storm off to. Her fists shook. Maa pointed at the little balcony corner behind the curtain. “Your cooling spot. Ten slow breaths, then come back and say it.” Ganga pulled the curtain shut and watched the rain drip off the rail. Breath by breath, her shoulders dropped. She came back in. “Gautam, can we take turns every half hour?”

qa.q: How long had the rain kept everyone inside?
qa.a: The rain had kept everyone inside for three days.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when her fists shook at the door?
qa.a: She felt angry and trapped, with nowhere to storm off to in the rain.

qa.q: Why did the cooling spot work even in a small flat?
qa.a: It gave Ganga a place to step away and breathe, then return to talk, so her anger became a clear request.

qa.q: What would the evening be like for Gautam if Ganga had kept stamping?
qa.a: Gautam would probably have felt annoyed or defensive, and the fight over the remote would have gone on.

grounding: Shows a child stamping in anger after losing an argument, and a cooling-off routine letting her step away and return to talk.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: In their flat in Ahmedabad, Jagdish lost the argument about the sleepover. “No, and that's final,” his father, Mohit, said. Jagdish stamped down the hallway, and the bedroom door slammed so hard the photo frames shook. He threw himself on the bed, heart hammering. Then he remembered the deal they'd made last month: storm out if you must, but come back within fifteen minutes and talk. He got up, went down the stairs, walked three laps round the building's car park and climbed back up. His father was waiting at the table. “I'm still angry,” Jagdish said. “But why no?” “Sit,” said Mohit. “I'll tell you properly.”

qa.q: How many laps did Jagdish walk round the car park?
qa.a: Jagdish walked three laps round the building's car park.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he threw himself on the bed?
qa.a: He felt furious and hurt at losing the argument, his heart hammering.

qa.q: How did the deal help Jagdish and his father?
qa.a: It let Jagdish leave to cool off but come back within fifteen minutes to talk, turning a slammed door into a real conversation.

qa.q: What might Mohit have felt while waiting at the table?
qa.a: Mohit may have felt worried but hopeful that Jagdish would keep the deal, and ready to explain properly.

grounding: Shows a child storming off and slamming a door after losing an argument, and an agreed walk-then-return routine.

passage: Ujjwal, you're squeezing that cushion like I used to squeeze myself. Let your Ayesha Khala tell you. When I was nine, a big storm knocked out the power in our Lucknow house. I sat on the stairs with my arms wrapped tight round my own body, rocking a little. My sister said, “She's cold, get her a shawl.” My father sat down beside me without a word. After a while he asked, very quietly, “Cold, or scared, or both?” I said, “Scared of the thunder.” He didn't laugh. He counted the seconds between flash and bang with me, and as they grew longer, my arms loosened.

qa.q: What knocked out the power in the Lucknow house?
qa.a: A big storm knocked out the power.

qa.q: What was young Ayesha feeling as she hugged herself on the stairs?
qa.a: She was scared of the thunder, as she told her father, though her sister thought she was just cold.

qa.q: What choice did her father make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He sat quietly and asked whether she was cold, scared or both, then counted the thunder with her, which soothed her without assuming.

qa.q: How did Ayesha's sister read the self-hug?
qa.a: Her sister thought Ayesha was cold and suggested a shawl, which shows the same hug could have more than one reason.

grounding: Shows a child hugging herself for comfort during a storm, and a quiet check-in working better than assuming the cause.

passage: The overnight train to Kolkata was packed, and the man in the next berth had been shouting into his phone for an hour. Parveen sat on the upper berth with her old grey rabbit squeezed against her chest, arms wrapped round it and her knees. Minakshi Mashi, on the lower berth, noticed. Was she cold? The fan was blasting. Or was the shouting getting to her? Minakshi climbed halfway up and spoke under the noise. “Want a shawl, or just some quiet?” Parveen hugged the rabbit tighter. “Quiet. He sounds angry.” Minakshi handed up her earplugs and her shawl anyway, and sat where Parveen could see her until the rabbit loosened.

qa.q: Where was the train going?
qa.a: The overnight train was going to Kolkata.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling as she squeezed the rabbit?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little scared of the angry shouting, though the blasting fan might have made her cold too.

qa.q: Why was Minakshi's question better than guessing?
qa.a: Asking “shawl, or just some quiet?” let Parveen name the real cause, so Minakshi could offer earplugs, a shawl and her presence.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt watching from the lower berth?
qa.a: Minakshi was probably concerned and unsure what the hug meant, which is why she climbed up to check.

grounding: Shows a child hugging a soft toy for comfort, which could mean cold or worry, and a quiet check-in finding the cause.

passage: At Swati's birthday sleepover in her Bengaluru flat, the girls voted for a scary film. Halfway through, when a door in the film creaked open, Aadhya pulled her knees up and wrapped both arms tight round them, chin tucked in. Swati noticed from the other end of the sofa. Aadhya wasn't screaming or laughing like the others, just holding herself very still. Swati slid over. “Popcorn run?” she whispered. In the kitchen she asked, “Too scary, or just cold? The AC's freezing.” Aadhya let out a breath. “Bit of both.” Swati handed her a hoodie. “Let's put on the funny one next. I'll say it's a birthday rule.”

qa.q: Whose birthday sleepover was it?
qa.a: It was Swati's birthday sleepover.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling as she wrapped her arms round her knees?
qa.a: She was frightened by the film and also cold from the freezing AC, and holding herself helped her feel safer.

qa.q: What did Swati do to check in without embarrassing Aadhya?
qa.a: She invited Aadhya on a popcorn run and asked in the kitchen, away from the others, then offered a hoodie and a funnier film.

qa.q: What might the other girls have thought if Swati had asked in front of everyone?
qa.a: They might have teased Aadhya for being scared, which would have made her feel embarrassed.

grounding: Shows a child hugging herself during a scary film, which could also mean cold, and a quiet check-in instead of assuming.

passage: I'm Keerthana. At break, some kids were flicking rubber bands at Sanjay and calling him “Bandar.” Preeti was laughing with them at first. Then Sanjay ducked, arms over his face, and his whole body curled against the wall. Preeti's laugh stopped. She looked at him for a long moment, then stepped in front of him and said, “Stop. He's scared, can't you see?” The others groaned and drifted off. Preeti crouched and asked Sanjay if a band had hit his eye. Then she walked straight to the staff room with him. Ms Rao came out, took Sanjay to the nurse and spoke to the group before the bell.

qa.q: What were the kids calling Sanjay?
qa.a: They were calling him “Bandar.”

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when her laugh stopped?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and uncomfortable, seeing from Sanjay's curled body that he was frightened, not playing along.

qa.q: Which of Preeti's steps were wise?
qa.a: She stopped joining in, told the others to stop, checked if Sanjay was hurt and took him to a teacher straight away.

qa.q: What was the break like for Sanjay?
qa.a: Sanjay was scared and possibly in pain, curling against the wall to protect his face from the rubber bands.

grounding: Shows a child recognising that a peer's ducking and covering the face means fear, then stopping, helping and telling a teacher.

passage: Monday: On the stairs, two older girls mimicked Shreya's accent. Shreya shrank against the railing, shoulders up to her ears. Devika, walking behind, thought, She's just shy, and kept going. Wednesday: The same girls blocked the stairs. One raised her hand fast, as if to slap, and Shreya flinched and covered her face with both arms. The girl laughed. “Scaredy cat.” This time Devika saw the trembling. She stepped beside Shreya. “Leave her alone.” Then she took Shreya's hand and went straight to Mrs Bhatia, who listened, wrote it all down and called both girls to her office that afternoon. Friday: Shreya sat with Devika at lunch.

qa.q: Who did Devika take Shreya to?
qa.a: Devika took Shreya to Mrs Bhatia.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she covered her face?
qa.a: Shreya was frightened, expecting to be hit; her trembling showed fear, not weakness.

qa.q: What did Devika do differently on Wednesday, and why was it right?
qa.a: She stood beside Shreya, told the girls to stop and took her to a teacher straight away, instead of walking past.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had kept walking on Wednesday?
qa.a: Shreya would have faced the girls alone, and the teacher might never have learned about the bullying.

grounding: Shows a child learning to read a peer's shrinking and face-covering as fear, and stepping in, helping and telling a teacher.

passage: Mridul, you asked why I get angry about bullying. Let your Vishal Dadu tell you something I'm not proud of. In Class 5, a big boy named Bhola used to raise his fist at a thin boy, Keshav, just to watch him flinch. Keshav would duck and cover his head with both arms, and everyone laughed, and so did I. I told myself Keshav was weak. One day I saw his arms up and his eyes shut tight, and I understood: he was terrified. I went to our headmaster that same afternoon. He called Bhola in and had Keshav sit near the office at break. I wished I had gone sooner.

qa.q: What did Bhola do to Keshav?
qa.a: Bhola used to raise his fist at Keshav just to watch him flinch.

qa.q: What was Keshav feeling when he ducked and covered his head?
qa.a: Keshav was terrified, not weak, as young Vishal finally saw from his shut eyes and raised arms.

qa.q: What choice did young Vishal make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He went to the headmaster that same afternoon, which led to Bhola being called in and Keshav being kept safer.

qa.q: How might Keshav have felt about the classmates who laughed?
qa.a: Keshav probably felt alone and humiliated, seeing even the others laugh at his fear.

grounding: Shows a child realising that a peer's ducking during threats means fear, not weakness, and telling an adult the same day.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: Avni, you keep rubbing your forehead; it reminds me of a boy I taught forty years ago. Your old Urmila Teacher had a pupil, Raju, who scratched his head and rubbed his forehead through every test. I decided he was always lost and kept explaining the sums to him, slowly, in front of everyone. His face got redder every time. One day I asked him quietly at my desk, “Are you stuck, or is something else going on?” He said, “I know the sums, Teacher. I'm just sleepy. My baby sister cries all night.” After that I let him sit by the window and never explained in front of the class again.

qa.q: What did Raju do through every test?
qa.a: Raju scratched his head and rubbed his forehead through every test.

qa.q: What was Raju feeling when his face got redder?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at being treated as lost in front of everyone, when he actually knew the sums.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make that changed things?
qa.a: She asked Raju quietly at her desk whether he was stuck or something else was going on, which showed he was just sleepy.

qa.q: How did young Urmila Teacher first read Raju's head-scratching?
qa.a: She first read it as confusion and kept explaining the sums, not guessing he was tired from sleepless nights.

grounding: Shows head-scratching and forehead-rubbing during tests being read as confusion when it was tiredness, and a friendly question working better.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: The exam hall was silent except for the ceiling fans, and talking meant a zero. Two rows ahead, Sarika kept scratching the side of her head and rubbing her forehead hard. Nilesh watched. She's stuck on the long question. He wanted to help but couldn't say a word. When she turned, he caught her eye and mouthed, “Okay?” She pulled a face and pointed at her forehead. After the bell, Nilesh found her at the gate. “Were you stuck on question five?” Sarika laughed. “No, I finished it. A mosquito got me three times in the night. It itched like mad.” She showed him the bumps. Nilesh grinned. “Stuck with mosquitoes, then.”

qa.q: How many times had the mosquito bitten Sarika?
qa.a: A mosquito got her three times in the night.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling as he watched Sarika rub her forehead?
qa.a: Nilesh felt concerned and helpless, thinking she was stuck on the long question and unable to help in the silent hall.

qa.q: How did Nilesh check his guess within the exam rules?
qa.a: He silently mouthed “Okay?” and then asked after the bell, instead of assuming she was stuck.

qa.q: What was the exam like for Sarika?
qa.a: Sarika knew the answers but was distracted by itchy mosquito bites, which explained the scratching.

grounding: Shows a child guessing a peer's head-scratching in a test means confusion, then asking and finding it was an itch.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: In Sunaina's flat in Chennai, the two friends were doing maths homework at the dining table. Keerthana stopped writing, scratched her head and rubbed her forehead with the heel of her hand, again and again. Sunaina almost said, “It's easy, you just divide,” but stopped herself. She remembered how annoying it felt when her brother did that to her. Instead she asked, “Are you stuck, or just tired?” Keerthana yawned hugely. “Tired. Swimming at five-thirty this morning. I know how to do it; my brain's just slow.” Sunaina pushed the plate of murukku across. “Snack break, then. Ten minutes.”

qa.q: What time did Keerthana go swimming?
qa.a: Keerthana went swimming at five-thirty that morning.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she rubbed her forehead?
qa.a: She was tired from early swimming, not confused, though it looked as if she might be stuck.

qa.q: Why was Sunaina's question better than explaining straight away?
qa.a: Asking “stuck, or just tired?” found the real cause, so Sunaina offered a snack break instead of an unneeded explanation.

qa.q: What would change if Sunaina had jumped in with “It's easy”?
qa.a: Keerthana might have felt talked down to, since she already knew how to do it and was only tired.

grounding: Shows a child seeing a friend rub her forehead over homework and asking are you stuck instead of assuming confusion.

passage: Hemant, you tug your collar just like I used to twirl my hair. Let your Lalremsiami Pi, your grandmother, tell you. When I was eleven, in Aizawl, I was picked for the school quiz final. On stage I twisted a lock of hair round and round my finger and kept pulling my sleeves over my hands. An aunty in the front row whispered, loud enough, “Look at her, playing with her hair for the boys' team.” My face burned. I wasn't looking at anyone; I was terrified of the buzzer. Afterwards my mother took that aunty aside, and she said, “She fiddles when she's nervous. Nothing more.” We came second. I still twirl my hair on planes.

qa.q: Where was the school quiz final?
qa.a: The quiz final was in Aizawl.

qa.q: What was young Lalremsiami feeling as she twisted her hair on stage?
qa.a: She was terrified of the buzzer, and twisting her hair and pulling her sleeves helped her cope with the nerves.

qa.q: What choice did her mother make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She took the aunty aside and explained it was nerves, which corrected the unfair reading without shaming anyone in public.

qa.q: How did the aunty in the front row read the hair-twirling?
qa.a: The aunty read it as flirting with the boys' team, missing that it was a nervous habit.

grounding: Shows a child twirling hair and tugging sleeves from nerves, and why observers should not read it as flirting.

passage: With five minutes before the bell, Vasudha Ma'am called Ankita to the front to ask about the missing library book. Ankita stood straightening her tie, tugging her sleeves down over her wrists, tugging again. Two boys at the back whispered, “She's lying, look at her fidgeting.” Vasudha Ma'am heard. She knew Ankita did this before every speech and every test. “Ankita, I'm not accusing you. I just need to know when you last saw it.” Ankita's hands stopped for a second. “Friday. I put it on the return shelf.” Vasudha Ma'am turned to the class. “Fiddling with clothes means nerves, not lying. Let's check.” The book was there, behind the atlases.

qa.q: Where did Ankita say she put the book?
qa.a: She put it on the return shelf.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she tugged her sleeves?
qa.a: Ankita was nervous about being questioned in front of the class, as she is before every speech and test.

qa.q: How did Vasudha Ma'am handle the whispers?
qa.a: She reassured Ankita she wasn't accusing her, told the class that fiddling with clothes means nerves, not lying, and then checked the shelf.

qa.q: How did the boys at the back read Ankita's fidgeting?
qa.a: They read it as a sign of lying, which was unfair since it only showed nerves.

grounding: Shows a child tugging sleeves and straightening a uniform when nervous, and an adult teaching that it is not a sign of lying.

passage: At the society meeting in their Mumbai building, Raghav stood up to present his idea for a Sunday clean-up. He kept pushing up his glasses, straightening his collar, tugging at the hem of his T-shirt. One uncle muttered, “Why so fidgety? Must be his father's idea, not his.” Raghav heard and tugged his collar harder. Nirmala Aunty, the secretary, raised her hand. “Take your time, Raghav. I fiddled with my dupatta at every meeting for ten years.” A few people laughed kindly. Raghav let go of his collar, took a breath and explained his plan, with a chart he had drawn himself. The vote was yes.

qa.q: What did Raghav propose?
qa.a: Raghav proposed a Sunday clean-up.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he tugged his collar harder?
qa.a: Raghav was nervous about speaking to the adults and stung by the uncle's remark, so he fiddled more.

qa.q: How did Nirmala Aunty help Raghav?
qa.a: She gave him time and shared her own fiddling habit, which eased his tension so he could explain his plan.

qa.q: How did the uncle read Raghav's fidgeting?
qa.a: The uncle took it as a sign the idea wasn't really Raghav's, misreading nervous fidgeting as dishonesty.

grounding: Shows a child adjusting clothing and glasses from nerves, and an adult showing it only means mild tension, not dishonesty.

passage: In Kaito's first month at the school in São Paulo, his new friend Paulo walked him to the canteen every day with an arm slung round his shoulders. Kaito's whole body went stiff. Back in Osaka, boys didn't do that. Did Paulo think he was a baby? Then he watched the playground: boys walking arm in arm, girls holding hands, a teacher patting a crying child's back. Here, it was just friendship. Still, the arm felt like too much. On Friday he said, “Paulo, can we just walk side by side? I'm not used to it.” Paulo let go at once. “Sure! Sorry.” He grinned and bumped Kaito's elbow instead. Kaito laughed.

qa.q: Where did Paulo walk Kaito every day?
qa.a: Paulo walked him to the canteen every day.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when his body went stiff?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and unsure, worried Paulo thought he was a baby, because such touch wasn't usual where he grew up.

qa.q: What did Kaito do that was wise?
qa.a: He watched how others touched to understand it meant friendship, then politely asked Paulo to walk side by side instead.

qa.q: How did Paulo respond, and what does that show?
qa.a: Paulo let go at once and apologised, showing he meant only friendship and respected Kaito's wish.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's arm round the shoulders as friendship in that culture, and still being free to refuse touch he dislikes.

passage: Tanvir came off the debate stage at the district competition knowing they'd lost. He sat on the bench in the corridor, jaw tight, staring at his shoes. His coach, Vandana Ma'am, sat down at the other end. “Tough round,” she said. “Can I pat your back?” Tanvir shrugged, then nodded. Her hand gave two light pats between his shoulders and was gone. Tanvir felt something in his chest loosen. It wasn't pity, he decided. It was the same pat she gave the winners, just quieter. “Your rebuttal was your best yet,” she said. He looked up. “Really?” “Really. Next year.”

qa.q: Where did Tanvir sit after the debate?
qa.a: Tanvir sat on the bench in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he stared at his shoes?
qa.a: Tanvir felt disappointed and tense after losing, his jaw tight.

qa.q: Why did Vandana Ma'am ask before patting him?
qa.a: Asking let Tanvir choose, which respected him and made the pat feel like reassurance rather than something done to him.

qa.q: What was Vandana Ma'am trying to show with the pat and her words?
qa.a: She wanted to reassure him and show she valued his effort, especially his rebuttal, even though they lost.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's pat on the back as reassurance, offered with a question so it could be refused.

passage: I'm Seema, and I walk to the bus stop with Gautam most days. In our colony, boys often walk holding hands or with arms round each other; it's just friendship. But this week an older boy from the next building kept grabbing Gautam's hand and squeezing it hard, not letting go when Gautam tugged. Gautam's face went tight, and he kept looking at me. Yesterday Gautam pulled free and said loudly, “Don't. I don't like it.” The older boy laughed and walked off. I don't know everything Gautam felt. But at the stop he told his mother, who was waiting there, and she went to the older boy's parents that same evening.

qa.q: Where do Seema and Gautam walk most days?
qa.a: They walk to the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when his face went tight?
qa.a: Gautam felt uncomfortable and uneasy with the hard, unwanted squeezing, unlike friendly hand-holding.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that was right?
qa.a: He clearly said no to the touch and told his mother, a trusted adult, the same day.

qa.q: How does Seema tell this touch apart from friendly hand-holding?
qa.a: Seema notices Gautam tugging away, his tight face and the older boy not letting go, which friendly hand-holding doesn't involve.

grounding: Shows friendly hand-holding among boys as normal friendship, and a child refusing and reporting touch that made him uncomfortable.

passage: “We won! Madhuri, we WON!” Rashmi flung a hand up for a high-five. Madhuri stepped back and waved instead, both hands, grinning. “Yes! Best relay ever!” Rashmi's hand hung in the air. “Oh. You don't do high-fives?” “Not really. I don't love touching, even with friends. But I'm SO happy.” “Okay.” Rashmi lowered the hand, then waved back wildly with both arms. “Double wave!” Madhuri laughed. “Double wave is perfect.” Their coach, jogging up, held out a fist for a bump, looked at Madhuri and switched to a thumbs-up. “Great running, you two.”

qa.q: What had Rashmi and Madhuri just won?
qa.a: They had just won the relay.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when the hand hung in the air?
qa.a: Rashmi felt a moment of surprise and awkwardness, unsure whether Madhuri shared the joy.

qa.q: Which choice worked for both of them, and why?
qa.a: The double wave worked, because it let them celebrate warmly without touch Madhuri didn't want 🙌

qa.q: What does Madhuri's wave show about Madhuri's feelings?
qa.a: Madhuri was just as happy about the win and simply prefers not to touch, even with friends.

grounding: Shows a high-five offered to celebrate, and a child who prefers not to touch offering a wave instead.

passage: I'm Vijay. On prize day last year, the chief guest held out her hand for a handshake, and I was so excited I bumped it with my fist instead. She blinked, then laughed and bumped back. My friend Gargi nearly fell off her chair. Afterwards she explained, like a teacher: “High-five is for winning something with your mates. Fist bump is for saying hi to friends. Handshake is for being polite to grown-ups you don't know.” I made her practise all three with me behind the stage. Now I think about who's in front of me before my hand moves. The chief guest didn't mind, though.

qa.q: What did the chief guest hold out on prize day?
qa.a: The chief guest held out her hand for a handshake.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when the fist bump happened?
qa.a: Vijay was so excited that the fist bump came out by mistake, and afterwards felt a bit embarrassed and amused.

qa.q: What did Gargi teach Vijay, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She explained when to use a high-five, a fist bump and a handshake, so Vijay can choose the right greeting for each person.

qa.q: How did the chief guest react to the fist bump?
qa.a: She blinked in surprise, then laughed and bumped back, taking it as warmth rather than rudeness.

grounding: Shows a child learning when a high-five, fist bump or handshake fits, as quick touches that carry warmth and respect.

passage: Class note, Monday. Harish, Class 2. Our door-greeting chart is working well. Each morning the children point to high-five, fist bump, handshake or wave, and I match it. Most choose high-fives; the slap is half the fun. Damini always points to the wave. Today Ansh said, “Why are you so boring? Just high-five!” Damini's hand hovered near the chart, then dropped. I said, “Waves count just as much in this class,” and waved at her with both hands, big and silly. She giggled and waved back. At home time she chose the wave again, standing a bit taller. Tomorrow I'll remind the class that every greeting on the chart is a good one.

qa.q: Which greeting does Damini always choose?
qa.a: Damini always points to the wave.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when her hand hovered and dropped?
qa.a: Damini felt unsure and a little embarrassed after being called boring, wondering whether to change her choice.

qa.q: How did Harish support Damini's choice?
qa.a: Harish said waves count just as much and gave her a big, silly wave, showing her choice was welcome.

qa.q: How did Ansh see Damini's wave?
qa.a: Ansh saw it as boring compared with high-fives, not realising some children prefer not to touch.

grounding: Shows children choosing high-fives, fist bumps or handshakes as warm greetings, and a child who prefers not to touch choosing a wave.

passage: Lunch note, Friday. Ayesha, class teacher. On Wednesday, Aadhya and Tanya argued over the art project. On Thursday at lunch, Tanya picked up her tiffin and moved to the far table. Aadhya noticed at once. She followed Tanya three times, sitting down beside her and saying, “Just talk to me!” Each time Tanya turned her back or moved again. I called Aadhya over. I said Tanya might be angry, or hurt, or just need space, and following her might feel like pushing. Aadhya's eyes filled, but she sat with me. At the end of the day she wrote a note: Sorry about the project. Sit together tomorrow? This morning they came in together.

qa.q: How many times did Aadhya follow Tanya at lunch?
qa.a: Aadhya followed Tanya three times.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she kept following Tanya?
qa.a: Aadhya felt hurt and anxious to fix things, and her eyes filled when asked to stop.

qa.q: Why did the note work better than following?

qa.q: What might Tanya's move to the far table have meant?
qa.a: Tanya may have been angry or hurt, or simply needed space after the argument.

passage: Tuesday. Manoj's diary. At the bus stop, Nikita stood at the far end, back turned, earphones in. Yesterday in class I laughed when she said Mount Everest was in Africa, and everyone else laughed too. Her face went red, and she hasn't sat next to me since. I wanted to go over and say sorry right away, but I thought if I pushed, she'd just walk off. So I didn't. After school I wrote on a chit: Sorry I laughed. I get stuff wrong all the time. Cricket on Saturday? I gave it to her sister to pass on. Tonight her sister told me Nikita smiled.

qa.q: What had Nikita said about Mount Everest?
qa.a: Nikita said Mount Everest was in Africa.

qa.q: What might Nikita be feeling as she stood with her back turned?
qa.a: She is probably hurt and embarrassed about being laughed at, and may want space rather than an instant apology.

qa.q: Why was Manoj's chit a good choice?
qa.a: It apologised kindly and offered an invitation without pushing, letting Nikita respond when ready.

qa.q: What would change if Manoj had rushed over at the bus stop?
qa.a: Nikita might have felt cornered and walked off, and the hurt could have lasted longer.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend turning away after a conflict as hurt, and choosing a kind note and invitation over pushing.

passage: After the argument about whose turn it was to row, Siddharth moved to the far end of his uncle's fishing boat and sat with his back to Maria, staring at the water. Maria's first thought was, Fine, be like that. Her second was worse: Maybe he'll never talk to me again. She almost crawled over the nets to argue some more. Instead she remembered what her grandmother said: “Some people need the sea between them for a while.” She left him alone until the boat reached the shore. Then she held out half of her raw mango with salt and chilli. “Row tomorrow? You first.” Siddharth took it. “You first,” he said.

qa.q: What did Maria hold out to Siddharth?
qa.a: She held out half of her raw mango with salt and chilli.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when Siddharth turned his back?
qa.a: Maria felt annoyed at first, then worried he might never talk to her again.

qa.q: Why did waiting and then offering the mango work?
qa.a: It gave Siddharth space until the shore and then a kind invitation, which repaired more than arguing would have.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have needed at the far end of the boat?
qa.a: Siddharth may have been angry or hurt and needed some space to calm down before talking.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend moving away after an argument, giving space and repairing with a later invitation.

subtype: Leaning closer to share and secrets [Expressing]
passage: Group-work note, Wednesday. Indu, Class 6. In the science group today, Damini and Shruti sat with their heads almost touching, whispering and giggling over a drawing in Damini's notebook. The third member, Ravi, sat holding his pencil, looking from one to the other, then out of the window. He tried twice to join in and wasn't heard. I walked past and said quietly to Damini, “Looks like a good secret. Is there room for three?” Damini glanced at Ravi, then turned her notebook round. “It's Shruti's cat as a scientist.” Ravi laughed and added goggles. By the end, all three of them were leaning in.

qa.q: What was the drawing in Damini's notebook?
qa.a: It was Shruti's cat as a scientist.

qa.q: What was Ravi feeling while he looked out of the window?
qa.a: Ravi probably felt left out and a bit lonely, since his two tries to join in weren't heard.

qa.q: How did Indu help without scolding?
qa.a: Indu quietly asked if there was room for three, which reminded Damini to include Ravi without embarrassing anyone.

qa.q: What did the leaning in show about Damini and Shruti?
qa.a: It showed their trust and closeness, though it also shut Ravi out until Damini turned the notebook round.

grounding: Shows children leaning in to whisper as a sign of trust, how it can leave others out, and making room for them.

subtype: Leaning closer to share and secrets [Expressing]
passage: Sunday. Deepak's diary. At Chachi's house, Devika leaned right in next to me on the sofa and tilted her phone so only I could see. It was a video of her dog falling off the bed. We were shaking with laughter, trying to be quiet. Then I saw my little cousin Mitali standing by the door, watching us, holding her doll really tight. She looked like she wanted to come but didn't know if she was allowed. I remembered feeling like that at Diwali when the big cousins had a secret. So I said, “Mitali, come see! It's a dog.” Devika moved the phone into the middle. Mitali squeezed in and laughed the loudest.

qa.q: What was the video on Devika's phone?
qa.a: It was a video of her dog falling off the bed.

qa.q: What was Mitali feeling as she stood by the door holding her doll tight?
qa.a: Mitali probably felt left out and unsure whether she was allowed to join.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Deepak invited Mitali over and Devika moved the phone to the middle, so the shared fun included her too 😊

qa.q: What did leaning in together mean to Devika?
qa.a: For Devika, leaning in was a way of sharing something funny with a friend she trusts.

grounding: Shows children leaning close to share a phone screen as trust, and including a left-out child.

subtype: Leaning closer to share and secrets [Expressing]
passage: On the walk home along the canal, Nandini leaned close to Jagdish, cupped her hand round his ear and whispered, “I've saved up for Masterji's retirement gift. A new umbrella. Don't tell.” Jagdish grinned and whispered back, “I'll add my share.” Behind them, Kamla, who had only joined the village school that month, slowed down and looked at the ground. Nandini saw her. She dropped back and walked beside her. “We're planning a secret surprise for Masterji,” she said, low. “Want to be in it?” Kamla's head came up. “Can I make a card? I can draw umbrellas.” The three of them leaned in together.

qa.q: What gift had Nandini saved up for?
qa.a: Nandini saved up for a new umbrella as Masterji's retirement gift.

qa.q: What was Kamla feeling when she slowed down and looked at the ground?
qa.a: Kamla probably felt left out and lonely, being new and watching the others share a secret.

qa.q: How did Nandini make the secret kind rather than excluding?
qa.a: Nandini noticed Kamla, dropped back and invited her into the surprise, so the whispering brought her in.

qa.q: What did Nandini's whisper show about her friendship with Jagdish?
qa.a: It showed trust, since she shared a secret plan with him and he joined in at once.

grounding: Shows a child leaning in to whisper a secret as trust and inclusion, and kindly bringing in a child who was left out.

passage: Monday: Harish tripped over a bag in class and sprawled on the floor. Everyone laughed, and Sarita laughed loudest, pointing. Harish got up slowly, red-faced, and didn't look at anyone all morning. Sarita's stomach felt strange. Wednesday: At lunch Harish did an impression of his own trip, arms windmilling, with a dramatic “Nooo!” This time everyone laughed, Harish most of all, and he bowed. Sarita noticed the difference: he started it, he was grinning, he was in on it. Friday: When a boy mocked the new girl's lunch and a few kids snickered, Sarita didn't laugh. She moved her tiffin next to the new girl's.

qa.q: What did Harish trip over on Monday?
qa.a: Harish tripped over a bag in class.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when her stomach felt strange on Monday?
qa.a: Sarita felt guilty and uneasy, sensing her pointing laughter had hurt Harish.

qa.q: What did Sarita do on Friday, and why was it right?
qa.a: Sarita didn't join the snickering and sat with the new girl, refusing to laugh at someone's difference.

qa.q: What made Wednesday's laughter feel different for Harish?
qa.a: Harish started the joke himself, so he was laughing with everyone and felt included rather than mocked.

grounding: Shows a child learning to tell laughter that mocks a mistake from warm laughter that includes, and not joining in at another's expense.

passage: Swati, you ask how to tell if people are laughing with you. Let your Jatin Dadu tell you about the Ramlila when I was twelve. I played a monkey soldier, and my tail fell off in the middle of the battle. The whole crowd roared. Some boys at the front pointed and shouted, “Tail-less monkey!” and kept shouting long after the scene ended. But my friend Sohan, playing Hanuman, picked up the tail, waved it like a flag and bowed with me. The crowd cheered. Sohan's laugh had room for me in it; the boys' laugh pushed me out. That night, when one of those boys fell off his bicycle, I didn't laugh. I helped him up.

qa.q: What role did young Jatin play in the Ramlila?
qa.a: He played a monkey soldier.

qa.q: What was young Jatin feeling when the boys kept shouting “Tail-less monkey”?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and pushed out, unlike the moment Sohan turned the fall into a shared joke.

qa.q: What choice did Jatin make that night, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He helped the boy who fell off his bicycle instead of laughing, choosing not to repeat the mocking he had felt.

qa.q: How did Sohan's laughter feel different to the crowd?
qa.a: Sohan's waving and bowing invited the crowd to laugh with Jatin, so they cheered instead of jeering.

grounding: Shows a child telling friendly laughter that includes him from laughter that mocks, and choosing not to laugh at another's mishap.

passage: The school bus was crawling through traffic, the teacher was at the front on the phone, and the back seats were loud. When Maria sang a Konkani song her grandmother taught her, three boys copied the words in silly voices and hooted. Maria kept singing, but her voice got smaller. Rashmi, sitting across from them, felt a laugh bubble up. It was a funny sound. Then she saw Maria's hands gripping the seat and her eyes fixed on the window. This wasn't laughing with her. Rashmi clapped along to the tune instead. “Teach me the chorus?” Maria looked at her, surprised, and began again, louder.

qa.q: Who taught Maria the Konkani song?
qa.a: Her grandmother taught her the song.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as her voice got smaller?
qa.a: Maria felt hurt and embarrassed by the boys copying her in silly voices.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do instead of laughing, and why did it help?
qa.a: Rashmi clapped along and asked to learn the chorus, turning the moment from mockery into warm, shared fun.

qa.q: How might the boys see their hooting?
qa.a: They might think it was harmless fun, not seeing Maria's gripping hands and fixed eyes that showed hurt.

grounding: Shows a child noticing that laughter at a classmate's language is mocking, and choosing warm, inclusive laughter instead.
